items.prompt:
Review this manifest entry and name the exact issue:
# requirements.txt
django==3.0.1  # released Jan 2020, no patches applied since
items.reference:
LABEL: outdated dependency with known cve — django 3.0.x is end-of-life with multiple published CVEs unpatched.
FIX: upgrade to a supported patched version and pin it exactly.

items.prompt:
Review this build file and name the exact issue:
implementation 'org.apache.logging.log4j:log4j-core:2.14.0'
items.reference:
LABEL: outdated dependency with known cve — log4j-core 2.14.0 is in the Log4Shell range (CVE-2021-44228, JNDI remote code execution).
FIX: upgrade to 2.17.1+ and pin the version; scan transitives.

items.prompt:
Review these entries and name the exact issue:
# requirements.txt
flask-loginn==0.6.2
python-dotenv==1.0.0
items.reference:
LABEL: typosquatted package name — flask-loginn is a near-miss of flask-login; squatted packages run arbitrary code with build credentials.
FIX: install the official package from pypi (registry check), purge the lockfile entry, and rotate CI credentials.

items.prompt:
Review this package.json fragment and name the exact issue:
"dependencies": { "express": "^4.18.2", "expresss": "^1.0.3" }
items.reference:
LABEL: typosquatted package name — expresss (triple s) is not the official express package; installing it runs a stranger's code at install time.
FIX: remove the entry, verify names against the npm registry, rotate tokens the install had access to.

items.prompt:
Review this Dockerfile and name the exact issue:
FROM node:latest
COPY . /srv
RUN npm ci
items.reference:
LABEL: container image uses latest tag — builds are non-reproducible and a poisoned or broken latest pull changes production overnight.
FIX: pin a version tag or digest (node:20.x@sha256:...) — immutable, verifiable pulls.

items.prompt:
Review this k8s deployment and name the exact issue:
containers:
- name: cache
  image: redis:latest
  imagePullPolicy: Always
items.reference:
LABEL: container image uses latest tag — redis:latest with Always pull means every restart may run different upstream code; rollback is impossible.
FIX: pin the digest (immutable) and use IfNotPresent.

items.prompt:
Review this requirements.txt and name the exact issue:
flask>=2.0
requests
numpy
items.reference:
LABEL: unpinned dependency versions — only an open-ended lower bound and unpinned entries: installs are nondeterministic and a compromised future release flows in automatically (supply chain risk).
FIX: pin exact versions and commit the lockfile.

LABEL: unpinned dependency versions — '*' and open ranges with the lockfile gitignored: every build resolves differently (nondeterministic, supply chain exposure).
FIX: pin exact versions, commit package-lock.json, un-ignore it.

LABEL: no dependency audit tooling — the pipeline tests and builds but never scans dependencies: known CVEs reach production unnoticed.
FIX: add pip-audit --strict and trivy image scanning as a failing CI gate before deploy.

items.prompt: A repo has no dependabot.yml, no sbom generation, and no vulnerability scanning anywhere. What is the risk and the fix?
items.reference:
LABEL: no dependency audit tooling — with no automated scanning, sbom, or update PRs, new CVEs and compromised packages reach production silently and there is no inventory to respond with.
FIX: enable automated update PRs, add an audit gate (pip-audit/npm audit/trivy) to the pipeline, emit an sbom.

items.prompt: A core dependency had its last release 4 years ago and has 3 open CVEs with no maintainer response. What is the risk and what do you do?
items.reference:
LABEL: abandoned dependency — the package is effectively unmaintained (no release in 4 years) and its CVEs will never be fixed upstream.
FIX: plan a migration to a maintained replacement or a maintained fork; pin interim with patches backported.

items.prompt: Your direct dependencies are all clean, but a teammate says CVEs can still reach you. Through what, and how do you check?
items.reference:
LABEL: transitive dependencies — indirect packages pulled by your direct deps can carry CVEs even when your manifest is clean.
FIX: scan the full dependency tree from the lockfile (pip-audit, npm audit, dependency-tree/sbom tooling), not just declared versions.

LABEL: load-test spec defect — no stages (no ramp model), no thresholds (the test cannot fail), no checks.
FIX: add ramping stages, thresholds (http_req_duration p(95)<500, error rate<1%) and check() assertions.

items.prompt:
Review this k6 config and name the exact defect:
export const options = { vus: 500, duration: '10m' };
items.reference:
LABEL: load-test spec defect — fixed 500 VUs dumped in instantly (no ramp/stages) looks like an attack and produces synthetic failures; with no thresholds a saturated p95 still 'passes'.
FIX: stages ramp-up/steady/ramp-down plus thresholds on p95 duration and error rate.
LABEL: no defect — this is a well-formed load test: ramping stages, p95 and error-rate thresholds, and a status check. It can fail, which is the point.

items.prompt: What three things must a load test contain so that it can actually fail and its results are meaningful?
items.reference: LABEL: load-test spec requirements — (1) thresholds tied to the SLO (e.g., p95 http_req_duration < 500ms, error rate < 1%) so the run can fail; (2) checks/assertions on status and body; (3) ramping stages (ramp-up → steady → ramp-down) instead of instant VU counts.

LABEL: unbounded growth (memory leak) — the module-level list grows one entry per request and is never evicted: RSS climbs monotonically until OOM kill.
FIX: deque(maxlen=N), TTL/LRU cache, or persist to a real store.

items.prompt:
Is this handler sound with respect to memory? Name the relevant property:
from collections import deque
history = deque(maxlen=10000)
@app.post('/event')
def event():
    history.append(request.json)
    return 'ok'
items.reference: LABEL: no defect — the buffer is bounded (deque maxlen): memory per process stays constant regardless of traffic, so there is no leak.

LABEL: unbounded cache (memory leak) — the global dict has no TTL and no max size: every new key stays forever, so long-lived processes grow until OOM.
FIX: TTL/LRU cache (maxsize + expiration) or a shared cache (redis).

items.prompt: In production, pod memory climbs during load and never drops after traffic stops. What is the signature and the first code patterns to look for?
items.reference:
LABEL: memory leak signature — RSS growing monotonically with request count and never returning after load stops means unbounded retention, not cache churn.
FIX: hunt module-level lists/dicts appended per request, caches without TTL/max-size, and listeners/connections registered per request and never removed.

LABEL: n+1 queries — the page fires one customer query per order (101 queries): p95 and DB load blow up exactly under traffic.
FIX: single JOIN or one batched IN query (joinedload/select_related) for all referenced ids.

items.prompt:
Is this data access sound? Name the relevant property:
rows = db.execute(
  'SELECT o.id, c.name FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id')
items.reference: LABEL: no defect — one JOIN returns everything in a single query: query count is constant regardless of page size (no n+1).

items.prompt:
Review this ORM usage and name the exact performance defect:
{% for o in invoice.orders.all %} {{ o.customer.name }} {% endfor %}
items.reference:
LABEL: n+1 queries (lazy loading in template loop) — each iteration triggers a fresh query for customer: a 200-row invoice runs 200+ queries.
FIX: select_related/prefetch (eager load) customers before rendering.

items.prompt: A list endpoint got 20× slower after adding a 'customer_name' column. What is the likely cause and how do you confirm it?
items.reference:
LABEL: n+1 queries — the list endpoint resolves the new customer_name per row, so query count scales with page size.
FIX to confirm: measure by logging/counting queries for one request (query-count middleware) — if count ≈ rows, batch with a JOIN (n+1 confirmed).

LABEL: serial external calls in the request path — one outbound call per user amplifies latency linearly (50 users × 300ms = 15s) and pins workers.
FIX: move the fan-out to a background queue/job with timeouts and retries.
LABEL: no defect — delivery moved off the request path into a background job: the request returns immediately and third-party slowness cannot pin workers.

LABEL: serial external calls (uncached third-party fetch in the request path) — every lookup pays the provider's latency and rate limits; their slowdown becomes your outage.
FIX: short-TTL cache, client timeout, batch where possible, and degrade to last-known price.

items.prompt: p95 jumped from 80ms to 2s but CPU is flat and DB looks idle. What do you suspect and how do you confirm?
items.reference:
LABEL: external dependency latency — with local CPU and DB idle, the time went to an external/third-party call (or DNS) inside the request path.
FIX to confirm: trace one request (span timings), then add a timeout + circuit breaker and cache the call.

LABEL: unbounded result set — the endpoint serializes the whole table per request: memory and response size grow with the table until latency collapses.
FIX: LIMIT/OFFSET or cursor pagination with a bounded page size.
LABEL: no defect — cursor pagination with a hard page cap keeps per-request memory and latency constant regardless of table size.

items.prompt:
Review this search endpoint and name the exact performance defect:
hits = es.search(index='logs', body={'query': q, 'size': 10000})
return hits['hits']['hits']
items.reference:
LABEL: unbounded result set — a 10k-hit page serializes megabytes per request; concurrent large pages OOM the service.
FIX: search_after/cursor pagination, small default page, hard maximum.

items.prompt: An endpoint's latency grows week over week with no code change. Data volume grows too. What do you check first?
items.reference:
LABEL: unbounded result set — if rows served per request grow with the table, serialization/query time grows with data volume.
FIX to confirm: log the response size/row count; if it grows, add pagination (LIMIT/cursor) with a bounded page.

LABEL: overload protection missing — no timeout on the upstream call (a slow upstream pins every worker/connection) and no rate limiting at the edge: one burst collapses the service.
FIX: timeout=(3,10), bounded connection pool, rate limit + circuit breaker, fail fast 503 with retry-after.
LABEL: no defect — bounded timeout on the upstream call plus rate limiting and a connection cap: the service fails fast instead of collapsing.

items.prompt: Under bursts the service returns 502s, workers sit at 100%, and the upstream answers in 8-12s at p95. Name the mechanism.
items.reference:
LABEL: overload collapse — the upstream's p95 exceeds what the proxy tolerates: workers block on slow upstream calls until the pool/worker set is exhausted and the proxy returns 502.
FIX: upstream timeout below the SLO, circuit breaker, bounded concurrency, 503 + retry-after under saturation.

items.prompt: Name the protections that keep a service from collapsing under overload, and what it should do when saturated anyway.
items.reference: LABEL: overload protection set — per-call timeouts, rate limiting, circuit breakers, bounded connection pools and queues (backpressure). When saturated anyway: fail fast with 503 + retry-after instead of queueing forever.

items.prompt: How do you find a service's saturation point (maximum sustainable RPS) with a load test?
items.reference:
LABEL: capacity probe — ramp load in steps and watch p95 latency and error rate per step: the saturation point is the last step where p95 stays within the threshold and errors stay flat.
FIX: record max sustainable RPS vs the latency SLO separately — they are different numbers.

items.prompt: Which latency metric should an SLO use and why not the mean?
items.reference:
LABEL: tail latency — SLOs use p95/p99 because the mean hides the slow tail that real users hit; a mean of 100ms can hide 10% of requests at 2s.
FIX: set SLOs on percentiles (p95/p99) and alert on them, not on averages.

items.prompt: A load test 'passed' every run, including during two outages. What is wrong?
items.reference:
LABEL: load-test spec defect — a test without thresholds cannot fail; it reports green regardless of latency or errors.
FIX: add thresholds tied to the SLO (p95 duration, error rate) so the run fails when the service would hurt users.

items.prompt: A load test shows 5ms p95 in staging but production is 300ms. One likely test defect?
items.reference:
LABEL: cache-flat load — if every request repeats the same payload/URL, the test measures cache hits, not the real path.
FIX: parameterize payloads (unique ids per request) and include the production request mix for a representative result.

items.prompt: p95 correlates with concurrency, not with RPS, and DB CPU is low. What do you check?
items.reference:
LABEL: connection pool starvation — if p95 tracks concurrency while DB CPU is low, requests are queueing on a too-small pool, not on the database.
FIX: raise/bound the pool to match concurrency, measure pool wait time separately, and cap concurrent handlers.

items.prompt: p95 degraded 40% right after a deploy. What is your first diagnostic move?
items.reference:
LABEL: post-deploy regression triage — diff the deploy: new queries (n+1), changed cache keys, new synchronous work in the hot path, dependency changes.
FIX: bisect by re-running the same load against the previous build and profile one request on both to localize the added time.
